articles.title: Why your custom post type URLs 404 (and how to never re-save permalinks again)
articles.excerpt: You register a custom post type, publish a post, open it, and get a 404. Nothing is wrong with your code. You go to Settings → Permalinks, click Save without changing anything, and now it works. Every…
articles.body: You register a custom post type, publish a post, open it, and get a 404. Nothing is wrong with your code. You go to Settings → Permalinks , click Save without changing anything, and now it works. Every WordPress developer learns this ritual eventually. Clients learn it too, usually right after a deploy. I finally got annoyed enough to find out exactly why it happens and to automate it away. This is what I learned. Routes are described in code but served from a cache When you call this: register_post_type ( 'recipe' , array ( 'public' => true , 'rewrite' => array ( 'slug' => 'recipes' ), ) ); WordPress doesn't create any URL rules yet. It records a permastruct ( /recipes/%recipe% ) in the global $wp_rewrite object.

articles.excerpt: Payments have a lifecycle, and a lifecycle with scattered update(status: ...) calls will eventually corrupt itself. I used AASM to turn our payment status handling into an explicit state machine, then…
articles.body: Payments have a lifecycle, and a lifecycle with scattered update(status: ...) calls will eventually corrupt itself. I used AASM to turn our payment status handling into an explicit state machine, then added row locking, idempotency, and a transition log to make it hold up under retries and duplicate events. Here is the problem, the approach, and the code. The problem: failures that kept coming back I worked on a Rails platform that handled recurring payments for renewals across multiple regions. Customers paid through bank (ACH) transfers and cards, and every payment had to stay consistent with a payment provider and an external CRM.

articles.title: Your app has native code even if you never wrote C++: the 16 KB page size check in 4 commands
articles.excerpt: Android devices have used 4 KB memory pages for as long as the platform has existed. Newer devices can run with 16 KB pages, and Google Play now requires apps to be ready for them. For an app with any…
articles.body: Android devices have used 4 KB memory pages for as long as the platform has existed. Newer devices can run with 16 KB pages, and Google Play now requires apps to be ready for them. For an app with any native code, including native code hidden inside a library, it can be a hard block on releasing updates. The trap The trap is assuming the app has no native code because you never wrote C++. Machine learning runtimes, video and audio libraries, database engines, image codecs and some analytics SDKs all ship .so files. If one of them was built for 4 KB pages only, your app is not compliant. The warning shows up in Play Console on someone else's code.

articles.excerpt: Flash Loan Attack Vector Analysis: HashKey Exchange Target Protocol: HashKey Exchange (TVL: $1547.3M) HashKey Exchange – Flash‑Loan Attack Vector Analysis Technical Security & Audit Report Prepared by…
articles.body: Flash Loan Attack Vector Analysis: HashKey Exchange Target Protocol : HashKey Exchange (TVL: $1547.3M) HashKey Exchange – Flash‑Loan Attack Vector Analysis Technical Security & Audit Report Prepared by: Senior DeFi Security Researcher Date: 15 Oct 2026 1. Executive Summary HashKey Exchange (HKEX) is a high‑throughput, order‑book‑style DEX operating on Ethereum L1 and several L2 roll‑ups, with a reported TVL of $1.547 B . Its core architecture combines an off‑chain matching engine with on‑chain settlement via a single “Settlement” smart‑contract that processes batched trades, updates liquidity pools, and distributes fees. Because the settlement contract is the sole on‑chain trust point, it is the primary target for flash‑loan‑driven manipulation .

articles.title: Windblown yardangs on Mars | Space photo of the day for Oct. 15, 2026
articles.excerpt: Martian sands blown by strong winds left rippled ridges on the surface of the Red Planet, as seen in this new image from the Mars Express spacecraft.
articles.body: A new image from the Mars Express spacecraft reveals windblown ridges known as yardangs, seen here as wrinkled sections on the left and right sides of the image. (Image credit: ESA/DLR/FU Berlin) A new image from the European Space Agency's Mars Express spacecraft reveals the powerful erosive forces that have shaped and re-shaped the surface of the Red Planet over long periods of geological time. What is it? This new Mars Express image captures Amazonis Mensa, a large, flat mountain on the Red Planet that offers planetary scientists a glimpse into the many factors that can sculpt a world's surface. In this photograph, several features stand out to help illustrate this. Easiest to make out are the large round craters created by ancient impacts on the surface of Mars .

articles.title: Beat light pollution with these six portable telescopes
articles.excerpt: Sick of skyglow spoiling your stargazing? These six telescopes are portable enough that you can easily pack them away and seek out darker skies.
articles.body: Light pollution is the astronomer's biggest enemy, especially if you're gazing into deep space. And while some of the best telescopes can make a difference, there's no way to eliminate it. That's why, if you want to observe the cosmos without obstruction, you need to seek out darker skies, get a smart telescope or combine the two. You don't have to book a flight to a dark sky reserve ; just traveling away from suburbia can be enough. That's where portable telescopes come in. Set one up in a field, for example, and you'll get a vastly improved view of the cosmos. Galaxies, nebulas and other deep space objects become more detailed when they're not washed out by skyglow.

articles.title: Scientists discover 'chemical starter kit' for life in planetary birthplaces
articles.excerpt: The discovery of surprising molecules of methanol and associated maser activity has expanded the inventory of the chemical starter kit that builds planets in young star systems.
articles.body: Methanol, coming as part of the 'chemical starter kit' around young stars, has produced some unexpected surprises that could ultimately reveal some of the conditions in which planets and potentially life form around protostars. The methanol discoveries were made by astronomers using ALMA (the Atacama Large millimeter/submillimeter Array) in the Atacama Desert in Chile, as part of a project called COMPASS (the Complex Organic Molecules in Protostars with ALMA Spectral Surveys). "Our work provides insight into the complex chemistry of young star systems and is ultimately an important piece of the puzzle in understanding the origin of life," said University of Bern astrophysicist Maria Drozdovskaya, who leads the COMPASS project, in a statement .

articles.title: SpaceX wants to launch Starship more than 450 times per year from South Texas
articles.excerpt: SpaceX has proposed increasing the number of allowed Starship launches from its Starbase site in South Texas from 25 per year to 456. The FAA is currently reviewing the request.
articles.body: SpaceX wants to start flying its Starship megarocket a lot more often. The company has requested permission to launch Starship from its Starbase site in South Texas up to 456 times per year. That's a big jump from the currently allowed cadence of 25. The U.S. Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) is in the early stages of reviewing the request. Today (Oct. 14), the agency announced "its intent to prepare a Programmatic Environmental Impact Statement, open a public scoping period and hold public scoping meetings for SpaceX’s proposal." Starship, which stands more than 400 feet (122 meters) tall, is the biggest and most powerful rocket ever built. It's also designed to be fully and rapidly reusable, a breakthrough that SpaceX believes will revolutionize spaceflight.

articles.title: Watch SpaceX deliver more than 6,000 pounds of cargo to the ISS today
articles.excerpt: SpaceX's CRS-35 cargo Dragon will rendezvous with the International Space Station today (Oct. 15) after a two-day chase. Here's how to watch it live.
articles.body: A Dragon is closing the gap between itself and its destination after a more than two-day-long orbital pursuit. SpaceX's cargo Dragon , flying the CRS-35 (35th Commercial Resupply Services) mission for NASA , is scheduled to rendezvous with the International Space Station (ISS) this morning (Oct. 15), delivering fresh food, long-term provisions, research and hardware to the orbital lab and its crew. Coverage of Dragon's arrival at the ISS will begin at 9:15 a.m. EDT (1315 GMT), with docking scheduled for approximately 11 a.m. EDT (1500 GMT). A livestream of the rendezvous will be available here and on Space.com's homepage, courtesy of NASA. SpaceX's CRS-35 launch creates a "space jellyfish" in the sky on Oct. 13.

articles.title: Anthropic warns small AI models could self-replicate through IoT devices
articles.excerpt: "Small weight-based replicators" could usher in a new generation of computer worms.
articles.body: AI company Anthropic is warning that advances in small AI models could soon usher in a new era of self-replicating malware that’s capable of infecting smart fridges, vacuum cleaners, and a wide range of other Internet of Things devices and is more resistant to takedown. By next year, smaller AI models may be able to autonomously self-replicate on all kinds of IoT devices, the company said. Eventually, the capability could enable computer worms, which propagate without requiring human interaction and are capable of infecting unfamiliar IoT devices. An experiment the company performed recently revealed significant challenges in bringing such an AI malware replicator to fruition, so the finding is necessarily tempered.
